        SECOND REPLY BRIEF OF JOINT CO-LOCATION DEVELOPERS

        Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) December 18,

2025 order (Co-Location Order),1 Eolian, L.P. (Eolian), Antora Energy, Inc., Calibrant Energy

(Calibrant), Mainspring Energy, Inc. (Mainspring), U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, and Verrus,

LLC (Verrus) (collectively, the Joint Co-Location Developers) submit this reply to the response

briefs filed in the captioned dockets on March 25, 2026. The brief draws upon the affidavit of

Andrew Levitt and Aniruddh Mohan of the Brattle Group on behalf of Eolian, at Attachment A.2

As highlighted in the Independent Market Monitor (IMM)’s response brief, PJM is proposing to

restrict the availability of non-firm contract demand service on the basis of vague reliability

concerns that are neither supported nor explained. But as the affidavit demonstrates, workable

non-firm service offerings that are broadly available are fully consistent with reliable system

operation, as demonstrated in other regions that are rapidly moving to implement non-firm

transmission service offerings.

        The Commission should not bow to the IMM’s and PJM’s thinly-supported attempts to

undermine the Co-Location Order. PJM’s proposal, if adopted, would fall short of the


1
 PJM Interconnection, LLC, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (Co-Location Order).
2

 Commission’s goal of “ensuring that all Americans (and all American businesses) have access to

affordable, reliable, and secure electricity.”3 As other regions are demonstrating, non-firm

transmission service holds significant potential to address the speed-to-power challenge while

maintaining a reliable electricity system. We therefore reiterate our request for the Commission

to require PJM to establish workable Non-Firm Contract Demand Service (Non-Firm CDS) rules

free from arbitrary and punitive terms that discourage their use, and Interim Network Integration

Transmission Service (Interim NITS) rules that allow load to rely on co-located supply if it is not

offering into the capacity market. By following through on the pathbreaking Co-Location Order,

the Commission can achieve its goals of ensuring that all loads can connect to the transmission

system in a timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory manner.

I.      ARGUMENT

        A.     A broad range of stakeholders support full implementation of the Co-
        Location Order.

        A broad range of stakeholders, representing the parties aiming to engage in co-location

arrangements as both load and generation, support robust implementation of the Co-Location

Order. Their support demonstrates that a broad range of developers stand ready to achieve the

Commission’s goals in the Co-Location Order of efficient and cost-effective load and generation

development should the Commission require PJM to enable a workable, fair, and reliable service

pathway. Specifically, these parties share our concerns that PJM and the PJM Transmission

Owners’ proposals contravene the letter and spirit of the Co-Location Order and the

Commission’s other requirements by:

     •   limiting the availability of Non-Firm CDS to generator outages;4

    •   limiting the ability of Interim NITS customers to serve their load from co-located

        generators during curtailment conditions;5

    •   setting the Non-Firm CDS rate at the same level as the higher-quality Firm Contract

        Demand Service (Firm CDS) rate;6

    •   threatening inadvertent misoperation with draconian penalties;7 and

    •   delaying implementation, without justifying why such delay is necessary.8

The Commission should address these concerns in adopting a replacement rate, directing PJM to

establish new transmission services that are commercially workable and therefore will result in

their widespread use.

        B.       The Commission must adopt a Grid Reliance Charge that is cost justified.

        In addition to these concerns, we also agree with Constellation, Vistra, and Geronimo

Power that the proposed Grid Reliance Charge “is derived from an unsound methodology that

violates cost causation principles”9—a point that we did not raise in our initial brief. The

testimony of Zachary Ming on behalf of Constellation explains that the PJM “Transmission

Owners attribute the full depreciation costs for a variety of transmission components (i.e. towers

and fixtures, poles and fixtures, overhead conductors, etc.) that are sized to meet the actual peak

do not impose any demand or withdraw any energy from the PJM system.”10

        The Joint Co-Location Developers stand ready and willing to pay our fair share of

transmission system costs. But part of the point of the new service framework is to reduce the

need for new transmission infrastructure. Rates for the new services should not be premised on

costs of infrastructure that is not needed to serve customers of these new services. Zachary Ming

proposes an alternate cost calculation framework that follows the Commission’s cost causation

principles.11 The Commission should direct the PJM Transmission Owners to adopt a Grid

Reliance Charge based on that methodology.

        C.      The Commission should not allow unsubstantiated reliability concerns to
        defeat implementation of the Non-Firm CDS product required by the Co-Location
        Order.

        The IMM leans heavily on PJM’s testimony to argue that PJM cannot reliably offer the

transmission services required by the Co-Location Order.12 PJM asserts that Non-Firm CDS must

be offered only “as a standby product” available “only ‘under limited circumstances.’”13 Its

position appears to rest on the unexplained premise that offering non-firm transmission service

under normal conditions involves widespread reliance on Remedial Action Schemes to control

withdrawals. Reliance on Remedial Action Schemes, PJM contends, will create “complexity”14

        PJM’s and the IMM’s claims are based on the mistaken assumption that increasing the

number of customers taking non-firm transmission service will proportionally increase system

reliance on Remedial Action Schemes. Rather, in the attached testimony, Levitt and Mohan

demonstrate that customers taking non-firm transmission service will not implicate widespread

reliance on Remedial Action Schemes because customers can instead generally rely on simpler

withdrawal-limiting protection systems internal to facilities to comply with curtailment

requirements.17 Further, Levitt and Mohan explain that PJM’s proposal to limit Non-Firm CDS

availability does not follow logically from its concerns with the reliability of Remedial Action

Schemes because PJM’s limitations will increase the time during which loads must rely on

facility-level protection systems and Remedial Action Schemes. Last, Levitt and Mohan show

that experience from other regions confirms that non-firm transmission service can be provided

without the limitations PJM seeks to impose. Specifically, Southwest Power Pool (SPP) and the

Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) are each developing non-firm services like those

envisioned in the Co-Location Order—and on a much faster timeline than that proposed by

PJM—without raising the purported reliability concerns that PJM and the IMM point to.18

          PJM contends that Non-Firm CDS should be offered only during a limited number of

hours due to reliability risks from over-reliance on Remedial Action Schemes.19 This argument is

flawed for several reasons.

         First, the IMM and PJM elide a distinction between simple withdrawal-limiting

protection systems that are required by PJM for sites taking non-firm transmission service, and

standard Remedial Action Schemes. Levitt and Mohan emphasize that there is an important

difference between the two.20 Unlike standard Remedial Action Schemes, which monitor and

control components across the grid, simple withdrawal-limiting protection systems monitor and

control only facility-internal components, monitoring flows, adjusting consumption or generation

at the site level, and disconnecting from the grid if necessary. In this way, while both systems are

designed to prevent unauthorized withdrawals from the grid, they operate at different levels of

the electrical grid. A facility-level protection scheme operates on a level comparable to a home’s

main circuit breaker. A standard Remedial Action Scheme is more like fast-acting air traffic

control—it reacts to events in one area to manage the flow across a different part of the system to

prevent overloads.

         This means that simple withdrawal-limiting protection systems can be relied upon much

more extensively than standard Remedial Action Schemes without creating the same

complexities and interdependencies.21 And in fact, reliance on simple withdrawal-limiting

protection systems under PJM’s proposal will extend beyond Non-Firm CDS customers:

customers taking Firm CDS while self-supplying a portion of their load will also rely on simple

 withdrawal-limiting protection systems to prevent withdrawals above their contracted level.22

Nevertheless, PJM does not impose limits on when a Firm CDS customer may self-supply a

portion of their load, nor does it voice concerns about the ability to serve Firm CDS customers

reliably.

         Second, PJM and the IMM ignore the redundancy built into the proposed service

construct. The co-location arrangements contemplated by the Co-Location Order entail

redundancy in the required protection systems.23 This redundancy is designed to protect against

failure and renders misoperation, already unlikely, even more improbable.

         Third, limiting the scope of Non-Firm CDS scheduling to generator outages, as PJM

proposes, will increase reliance on simple withdrawal-limiting protection systems rather than

decrease it. This is because withdrawal-limiting protection systems are only active when the

customer cannot withdraw, i.e., because no transmission service has been scheduled. By limiting

Non-Firm CDS to periods of generator outage, PJM’s proposal increases the frequency with

which a customer will not be authorized to withdraw, thereby increasing the time for which such

mechanisms must be relied upon. As Levitt and Mohan explain, “[i]t therefore follows that

narrowing eligibility for N[on] F[irm] CDS scheduling does not decrease complexity.”24

         Fourth, to the extent that PJM is concerned about managing the potential for interactions

among standard Remedial Action Schemes that are monitoring and controlling elements on the

bulk transmission system (as distinct from simple withdrawal-limiting protection systems), it

place, and instead maximize use of pre-contingency Non-Firm CDS curtailment through

scheduling.25 Reliance on pre-contingency curtailment is similar to how SPP and ERCOT

envision curtailment under the non-firm transmission services that they are developing, described

in further detail below.

         For these reasons, PJM’s and the IMM’s concerns do not “call for relying on” Non-Firm

CDS “as a standby product” only.26 The Commission should instead require PJM to establish a

Non-Firm CDS product consistent with the requirements of the Co-Location Order.

                  2.     Non-firm transmission services proposed by SPP and ERCOT show
                  that non-firm transmission service can be offered reliably.

         Other grid operators are developing non-firm transmission service options without the

limitations that PJM and the IMM claim are needed.27 Specifically, SPP and ERCOT are

developing non-firm services similar to those proposed in the Co-Location Order, showing that

non-firm service can be offered reliably on an as-available basis and implemented quickly.

         Levitt and Mohan explain that SPP recently filed tariff revisions in Docket No. ER26-

1323 to offer a new non-firm Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (CHILLS) that would

allow non-firm transmission service that is curtailable in the face of insufficient transmission

capacity.28 Unlike PJM’s Non-Firm CDS product, however, SPP plans to make CHILLS broadly

available during all non-constrained hours, rather than limit use to periods when an associated

Moreover, the SPP Transmission Owner Group supports CHILLS, explaining that “CHILLS has

maintain grid reliability.”32 The SPP Market Monitoring Unit also supports acceptance of SPP’s

         Levitt and Mohan also explain that ERCOT staff have developed a proposal by which a

Provisional Controllable Load Resource (P-CLR) can withdraw power from the transmission

network on a non-firm basis and subject to curtailment as part of ERCOT’s ongoing “Batch

Controllable Load Resource (CLR) construct enables curtailment of loads on a nodal basis in

security-constrained economic dispatch (SCED) for resolving constraints.35 The P-CLR proposal

builds on the CLR construct by allowing loads to accelerate interconnection if they choose to use

the transmission system on an as-available basis and curtail to resolve constraints as necessary.36

Importantly, Levitt and Mohan note that PJM’s Non-Firm CDS would include more reliability

        SPP’s and ERCOT’s proposed non-firm transmission service offerings show that

transmission service can be provided on a non-firm and as-available basis. PJM’s own proposed

implementation of Interim NITS also demonstrates that non-firm transmission service need not

be limited to periods of outage for the co-located generator as PJM has proposed for Non-Firm

CDS. While PJM’s Interim NITS proposal suffers from other flaws, PJM has proposed to make it

broadly available during normal operating conditions, and has not claimed that doing so will

compromise reliability.

        SPP and ERCOT have also shown that non-firm transmission service can be implemented

quickly. Unlike PJM’s requested 2029 effective date, SPP requested a July 1, 2026 effective date

for CHILLS,38 while ERCOT hopes to implement P-CLRs as soon as 2027.39 Neither PJM nor

the IMM has described any PJM-specific conditions that would prevent PJM from promptly

offering non-firm transmission service available during normal conditions in a similar manner to

SPP or ERCOT.

                 3.     The Commission must enforce the requirements of the Co-Location
                 Order.

        The Co-Location Order proposed a commonsense solution to a critical and pressing

problem. The Commission must not allow unsubstantiated reliability concerns to dilute or delay

the Co-Location Order’s promise. Instead, the Commission must reject PJM’s attempt to limit

  1   I.        QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Our names are Andrew Levitt and Aniruddh Mohan. We have previously submitted the Affidavit
 3   dated March 25, 2026, in this Docket EL25-49-000 et al.


 4   II.       ASSIGNMENT

 5   We were asked by Eolian, L.P. to supplement our Affidavit dated March 25, 2026, to offer
 6   additional perspectives on the reliability and timeline implications of the proposed new
 7   transmission services in PJM’s Initial Brief in Docket No. EL25-49-000 et al.


 8   III.      BACKGROUND

 9   As part of its compliance filing to FERC in Docket EL25-49-000, in February 2026, in an
10   accompanying Initial Brief, PJM set out illustrative tariff language and supporting positions for
11   three new service categories for generators serving co-located load: Non-Firm Contract Demand
12   Transmission Service (“Non-Firm CDS” or “NFCDS”), Interim Network Integration
13   Transmission Service (“Interim NITS”), and Firm Contract Demand Service (“Firm CDS”).1
14   PJM also submitted supporting affidavits addressing planning, operations, market design, and
15   implementation timing.

16   Since then, a number of stakeholders have submitted responses to PJM’s Initial Brief. We submit
17   this Supplemental Affidavit in response to the timing and transmission reliability issues PJM and
18   other stakeholders have raised before the Commission regarding the impact of non-firm services.


19   IV.       SUMMARY

20   Since PJM has taken steps in its Initial Brief and compliance filing to create new transmission
21   services for co-located loads, a minority of stakeholders have raised concerns that provision of
22   these new transmission services would be inconsistent with the safe and reliable operation of the

  1   transmission system.2 In this Supplemental Affidavit, we find that the concerns raised do not
 2   provide evidence that provision of NFCDS or Interim NITS would be inconsistent with reliable
 3   system operations. To the contrary, we point to similar non-firm services developed in other
 4   regional transmission organizations (“RTOs”) as evidence that such services can be offered and
 5   implemented reliably. We also note that non-firm services being developed in other RTOs have
 6   many of the enhancements we previously proposed to PJM in our prior Affidavit dated March
 7   25, 2026. We then note that these services in other RTOs are being implemented on a faster
 8   timeline than that proposed by PJM. Moreover, PJM has long provided non-firm point-to-point
 9   transmission service without causing the reliability concerns voiced by these stakeholders.

10   We also find that PJM’s Initial Brief and its Supporting Affidavits have made unclear and often
11   conceptually inconsistent arguments regarding the reliability implications of Interim NITS and
12   NFCDS that have led to comments citing potential risks from provision of non-firm service.3
13   PJM suggests that its requirement to use protection systems to limit withdrawals at facilities
14   taking CDS implies complexity that warrants narrow limitations on scheduling of NFCDS. The
15   PJM Independent Market Monitor has asserted that, due to complexity, extensive deployment of
16   NFCDS could become “unmanageable.”4 However, we show that PJM’s argumentation is
17   flawed, that NFCDS scheduling therefore could be allowed at any time without increasing
18   complexity from protection systems (and potentially reducing it), and that the use of the required
19   protection systems does not imply any reliability issues due to widescale adoption of CDS.

20   In particular, PJM’s Initial Brief does not sufficiently distinguish between types of protection
21   systems. For facilities taking CDS, the protection system required by PJM monitors and controls
22   conditions internal to those facilities in order to limit withdrawals at all times. By contrast, a
23   standard Remedial Action Scheme (RAS) monitors and controls disparate parts of the bulk
24   transmission system to avoid overloads there. Even though standard RAS is not required for a

  1            V.A.       SPP CHILLS shows non-firm service is workable and does not
 2                       create significant reliability concerns

 3   Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) recently filed with FERC, in Docket No. ER26-1323-000, tariff
 4   revisions to offer a new non-firm transmission service called Conditional High Impact Large
 5   Load Service (“CHILLS”).8 Similar to PJM’s proposed NFCDS and Interim NITS, load that is
 6   served under CHILLS does not have firm access to the transmission system, and SPP has no
 7   obligation to serve the load if insufficient transmission capacity exists. In SPP’s filing to FERC,
 8   Part VII § 44.4 states that: “The Transmission Provider and Transmission Owners undertake no
 9   obligation under the Tariff to plan the Transmission System in order to have sufficient capacity
10   for CHILLS”;9 CHILLS “is subject to availability and to Curtailment or Interruption”; “[t]he
11   Transmission Customer or the Network Customer must not withdraw energy from the
12   Transmission System at the CHILL delivery point that exceeds its CHILLS Reserved Capacity”;
13   and “The Transmission Customer or the Network Customer must fully respond to a load shed or
14   curtailment for the CHILL delivery point directive by the Transmission Provider.”10 In both grid
15   planning and operations this is broadly similar to PJM’s proposed design of NFCDS and Interim
16   NITS: for example PJM states in its illustrative tariff that both NFCDS and Interim NITS are
17   “non-firm” and “interruptible.”11 In a supporting affidavit, Dr. Abdulsalam notes that the
18   transmission system is not planned for NFCDS: “this load is neither planned for (i.e., PJM’s
19   transmission planning does not consider this load and so the system is not designed to
20   accommodate it)” showing consistency with SPP’s CHILLS.12

 4   of CHILLS in SPP directly contradicts the PJM IMM’s claim that implementation of non-firm
 5   service would be unworkable and create significant reliability risks. The PJM IMM does not
 6   point to specific planning or operational reasons why PJM offering NFCDS and Interim NITS, as
 7   directed by the Commission’s Co-Location Order, would create reliability concerns, even though
 8   SPP can reliably implement such a service.15

 9   We also note that SPP does not limit the reservation of CHILLS to periods in which an
10   associated generation resource is on outage, unlike PJM’s proposed implementation of NFCDS.
11   Rather, SPP plans to make CHILLS broadly available during all hours. In addition, in contrast to
12   PJM’s description of its Interim NITS offering to stakeholders,16 SPP does not restrict customers
13   taking CHILLS from relying on co-located capacity or energy during periods of system tightness
14   and supply adequacy shortfalls.17 All of this suggests that PJM’s Interim NITS and NFCDS
15   service is not only workable and able to be reliably implemented, but can in fact be further
16   enhanced for broader uptake and commercial viability. We detail these enhancements in our
